entity.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
entity.description: The child prodigy who summed 1 to 100 in seconds and became the greatest mathematician of his era. Gauss proved how to construct a 17-sided polygon at 19, tracked the dwarf planet Ceres from just three observations, and co-invented the electromagnetic telegraph. Over 100 mathematical concepts bear his name, yet he famously refused to publish work he considered incomplete.

story.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
story.description: A butcher's son stuns his teacher by summing 1 to 100 instantly, proves a 2,000-year-old geometry problem at 19, predicts the orbit of a lost dwarf planet, and co-builds the first electromagnetic telegraph. The prince of mathematicians.

moments.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss Is Born to a Bricklayer's Family in Brunswick
moments.subtitle: A child prodigy emerges from poverty to become the prince of mathematicians
moments.description: On 30 April 1777, Carl Friedrich Gauss was born in Brunswick, in the Duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttel. His father worked as a butcher, bricklayer, and gardener, and his mother was nearly illiterate. Gauss showed astonishing mathematical ability from early childhood. An apocryphal but widely told story recounts that his elementary teacher asked the class to sum the numbers 1 to 100; young Gauss instantly answered 5,050 by recognizing the sum as 50 pairs of 101. His teachers brought him to the attention of the Duke of Brunswick, who sponsored Gauss's education through university, launching one of the most extraordinary mathematical careers in history.

moments.name: A 19-Year-Old Gauss Proves How to Construct a 17-Sided Polygon
moments.subtitle: The first advance in regular polygon construction since the ancient Greeks, 2,000 years earlier
moments.description: On 30 March 1796, while a student at the University of Gottingen, 19-year-old Carl Friedrich Gauss proved that a regular 17-sided polygon (heptadecagon) could be constructed using only a compass and straightedge. This was the first progress on the problem of regular polygon construction in over 2,000 years, since the ancient Greeks had solved only the cases of 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 15 sides. The discovery convinced Gauss to pursue mathematics instead of philology as a career. He began his mathematical diary that day, recording results that would form the basis of his masterwork Disquisitiones Arithmeticae.

moments.name: Gauss Predicts the Orbit of the Lost Dwarf Planet Ceres from Just Three Observations
moments.subtitle: Astronomers lose a planet; a mathematician finds it using brand-new math
moments.description: In late 1801, Carl Friedrich Gauss calculated the orbit of the dwarf planet Ceres after it had been observed briefly by Giuseppe Piazzi in January and then lost behind the Sun. Using only three observations spanning 41 days, Gauss applied his newly developed method of least squares to predict where Ceres would reappear. When astronomers pointed their telescopes to Gauss's predicted position on 31 December 1801, Ceres was found almost exactly where he said it would be. The feat made the 24-year-old Gauss internationally famous and demonstrated the power of mathematical methods in astronomy.

moments.name: Gauss and Weber Build the First Electromagnetic Telegraph in Gottingen
moments.subtitle: Two physicists string a wire between their buildings and invent instant communication
moments.description: In 1833, Carl Friedrich Gauss and physicist Wilhelm Eduard Weber constructed the first electromagnetic telegraph, connecting the Gottingen Observatory where Gauss worked to Weber's physics laboratory about 1.5 kilometers away. The device used a galvanometer to detect changes in magnetic field strength caused by electrical signals sent through the wire. While Samuel Morse's telegraph later became the commercially dominant design, the Gauss-Weber telegraph was the first working electromagnetic communication system. In the same year, Gauss also invented the magnetometer and made the first absolute measurement of Earth's magnetic field.

moments.name: Gauss Dies in His Sleep at the Gottingen Observatory After 48 Years as Director
moments.subtitle: The prince of mathematicians passes away in the building where he spent half his life
moments.description: On 23 February 1855, Carl Friedrich Gauss died in his sleep at the Gottingen Observatory, where he had served as professor of astronomy and director since 1807. He was 77 years old. Gauss had lived and worked in the observatory building for nearly half a century, making fundamental contributions to number theory, algebra, statistics, astronomy, geodesy, and electromagnetism. He had married twice, fathered six children, and trained students including Bernhard Riemann and Richard Dedekind. More than 100 mathematical and scientific concepts bear his name, an unrivaled legacy in the history of science.
